arml-local-2018-individual-02.title: Constant sequence
arml-local-2018-individual-02.body:
""The answer must not depend on the sequence, so take the constant sequence $a_n=a_0$: $18a_0+20=20a_0+18$ gives $a_0=1$.

**Answer: 1**

arml-local-2018-individual-04.title: Least common multiple of periods
arml-local-2018-individual-04.body:
""$\sin\left(\frac{\pi x}3\right)$ has period $6$ and $\cos\left(\frac{\pi x}2\right)$ has period $4$, so $12=\operatorname{lcm}(6,4)$ is a period of $f$.

It is the least one: the two summands have different frequencies, so $f(x+p)-f(x)\equiv0$ forces each summand to repeat separately (a sum of sinusoids of distinct frequencies vanishes identically only if each term does). Then $p$ is a multiple of both $6$ and $4$, hence of $12$.

**Answer: 12**

arml-local-2018-individual-05.title: Use the lcm
arml-local-2018-individual-05.body:
""The product must be a multiple of $\operatorname{lcm}(20,18)=180$. One of the three numbers is a multiple of $5$, say $m$; if $d=\gcd(m,180)$, the other two numbers must have a product divisible by $\frac{180}d$. Checking $m=5,10,\dots,45$ (and the triples containing them) gives exactly:

- $m=10$: $8,9,10$
- $m=20$: $18,19,20$
- $m=35$: $34,35,36$ and $35,36,37$
- $m=45$: $43,44,45$ and $44,45,46$

That is $6$ triples (every number is below $50$).

**Answer: 6**

arml-local-2018-individual-07.title: Subtract the singular ones
arml-local-2018-individual-07.body:
""There are $6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=360$ matrices $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ with distinct entries from $S$. It is singular iff $ad=bc$. Two products of distinct elements can coincide in only two ways with four distinct numbers: $1\cdot6=2\cdot3$ and $2\cdot6=3\cdot4$. For each of these, $a$ can be any of the four numbers; this fixes $d$ (the partner in the same product), and then the other pair fills $b,c$ in $2$ ways: $4\cdot2=8$ singular matrices per set, so $16$ in all.

Invertible: $360-16=344$.

**Answer: 344**

arml-local-2018-individual-08.title: Coordinates
arml-local-2018-individual-08.body:
""Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so $EF$ passes through the midpoint of $AC$, the center of the rectangle. Put the center at the origin with $A=\left(-\frac{19}2,-\frac{15}2\right)$, $B=\left(-\frac{19}2,\frac{15}2\right)$, $C=\left(\frac{19}2,\frac{15}2\right)$, $D=\left(\frac{19}2,-\frac{15}2\right)$, and $E=(x,y)$, $F=(-x,-y)$.

The shoelace formula gives $[AECF]=|15x-19y|=107$ and $[BEDF]=|15x+19y|=88$. Taking $y>0$ without loss of generality, either

- $15x-19y=-107$, $15x+19y=-88$: $x=-\frac{13}2$, $y=\frac12$; or
- $15x-19y=-107$, $15x+19y=88$: $x=-\frac{19}{30}$, $y=\frac{195}{38}$.

Since $EF=2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, the first is larger: $EF=2\sqrt{\frac{169}4+\frac14}=\sqrt{170}$. (Both points are inside the rectangle, as $|x|<\frac{19}{2}$, $|y|<\frac{15}{2}$.)

**Answer: $\sqrt{170}$**

arml-local-2018-individual-09.title: Reduce to coprime $a,b$
arml-local-2018-individual-09.body:
""Dividing $a,b$ by their gcd, we may assume $\gcd(a,b)=1$. Then $a$, $b$, $a+b$ are pairwise coprime and all divide $N$, so $ab(a+b)\mid N$.

Numbers of the form $ab(a+b)$ with $1\le a<b$ coprime and at most $100$: $6\,(1,2)$, $12\,(1,3)$, $20\,(1,4)$, $30\,(1,5)$ and $(2,3)$, $42\,(1,6)$, $56\,(1,7)$, $70\,(2,5)$, $72\,(1,8)$, $84\,(3,4)$, $90\,(1,9)$. Discarding those that are multiples of smaller ones, the minimal ones are $6,20,56,70$.

So $N$ qualifies iff it is a multiple of one of $6,20,56,70$ (and $\le100$): $\lfloor100/6\rfloor=16$ multiples of $6$; the multiples of $20$ not already multiples of $6$: $20,40,80,100$ ($60$ is a multiple of $6$), giving $4$ more; then $56$ and $70$ give $2$ more. Total $16+4+2=22$.

**Answer: 22**

arml-local-2018-individual-10.title: Geometric sum in exponentials
arml-local-2018-individual-10.body:
""$$\frac{\sin 10x}{\sin x}=\frac{e^{10ix}-e^{-10ix}}{e^{ix}-e^{-ix}}=e^{9ix}+e^{7ix}+\dots+e^{-7ix}+e^{-9ix}.$$
Squaring and collecting equal exponents (the exponent $2m$ arises from $10-|m|$ pairs), the square equals
$$\left(e^{18ix}+e^{-18ix}\right)+2\left(e^{16ix}+e^{-16ix}\right)+\dots+9\left(e^{2ix}+e^{-2ix}\right)+10,$$
which is $2\cos18x+4\cos16x+\dots+18\cos2x+10$.

So $a_0=10$, $a_{2k}=2(10-k)$ for $k=1,\dots,9$ (i.e. $18,16,\dots,2$), and the odd-indexed $a_i$ are $0$. Hence
$$\sum a_i^2=10^2+(2^2+4^2+\dots+18^2)=100+4\cdot285=1240.$$

**Answer: 1240**

arml-local-2018-individual-11.title: Pair $c$ with $48-c$
arml-local-2018-individual-11.body:
""Rewrite as $P_c(x)=cx^9-x^5-x^4+(48-c)=0$. Then
$$P_{48-c}(x)=(48-c)x^9-x^5-x^4+c=x^9P_c\!\left(\tfrac1x\right),$$
so (the roots being nonzero) $x$ is a root of $P_c$ iff $\frac1x$ is a root of $P_{48-c}$. As the real root is unique, $f(c)f(48-c)=1$ for $c\ne48$.

Hence the product over $c=1,\dots,47$ pairs up into $f(c)f(48-c)=1$ for $c\ne24$, leaving $f(24)$: from $x=-1$, $\frac{-1+1-48}{-1-1}=24$, so $f(24)=-1$. Finally $f(0)=2$ since $\frac{32+16-48}{511}=0$.

The product is $f(0)\cdot f(24)\cdot1=2\cdot(-1)=-2$.

**Answer: $-2$**
